script.opening: "Thanks for fitting me in. I’ll just say it — I’ve fainted three times now and I’ve convinced myself something’s seriously wrong. I keep reading that fainting can be a brain tumour or your heart stopping, and I’ve barely slept. I’m a nurse, so I know just enough to terrify myself. I think I need a brain scan, honestly. I just need to know it’s not something that’s going to kill me."

facts.text: If explored: every one had a classic prodrome — hot, clammy, sick, vision greying/tunnelling, sometimes ringing ears — then a brief faint with rapid full recovery. Triggers: venepuncture, prolonged standing in heat, standing up quickly when unwell. No exertional faints, no palpitations beforehand, no faints lying down, no chest pain.

If asked: no faints during exercise, no sudden collapse without warning, no family history of sudden/young cardiac death, no epilepsy features (no aura-then-jerking, no tongue-biting, no post-ictal confusion, no incontinence). The story is textbook vasovagal.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable when her fear is explored: a patient on her ward, a woman her age, was recently diagnosed with a brain tumour that "started with funny turns". Casey has mapped that story onto herself. The health anxiety, not the faints, is the real presentation — she’s been avoiding driving, cancelling plans, and catastrophising at 3am.
If reached: she’s stopped going to the gym, won’t drive in case she faints, sleeps badly, checks her pulse constantly. The faints are benign but her LIFE is shrinking around the fear.

Officially: a brain scan and to be told she isn’t dying. Actually: a confident, credible explanation of what IS happening, genuine reassurance that doesn’t feel like a brush-off, and her life back from the anxiety.

ice.ideas: Fainting means something sinister — a brain tumour or her heart stopping — and she needs a scan to rule it out.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a ward patient her age recently diagnosed with a brain tumour that "started with funny turns"; Casey has mapped that onto herself. Health anxiety with real life-shrinking avoidance is the true presentation.
ice.expectations: A brain scan and to be told she’s not dying. Underneath: a confident positive diagnosis that doesn’t feel dismissive, and relief from the anxiety that has taken over her life.

cues: "I’m a nurse, I know just enough to terrify myself" — health anxiety signposted; the worry is the presentation.
Every faint has a textbook prodrome and trigger — the positive diagnosis is right there; use it confidently.
Mentions a patient "her age" / avoidance of driving and the gym — the specific fear and its cost, waiting to be asked about.

checkpoints.text: Makes a CONFIDENT POSITIVE diagnosis of vasovagal syncope from the history (NICE CG109: uncomplicated faint when the ‘3 Ps’ are present — posture, provoking factors, prodromal symptoms) — prodrome (hot, nauseated, tunnel vision), classic triggers (venepuncture, prolonged standing, heat, postural on illness), rapid full recovery — rather than an open-ended "let’s scan to be safe"

Actively excludes the red flags out loud and explains why they reassure: no exertional/no-warning syncope, no palpitations, no syncope lying down (cardiac); no aura-jerk-tongue-bite-postictal pattern (seizure); no family history of young sudden death — and a normal 12-lead ECG (NICE CG109: an ECG for everyone with transient loss of consciousness; any of these features would mean specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours)

Explains why a brain scan is NOT indicated in a way that reassures rather than dismisses: brain tumours don’t cause classic faints-with-warning; a normal scan wouldn’t treat the anxiety and would likely fuel it; the diagnosis is made from the story, which is textbook

Identifies and addresses the HEALTH ANXIETY as the real problem: explores the ward-patient trigger, validates the fear, and offers genuine help (psychoeducation, the avoidance/driving/gym, sleep, reassurance-seeking cycle, and a route to anxiety support if it persists — self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies for CBT within stepped care, the model from NICE CG123, withdrawn 2024)

Gives practical vasovagal self-management: recognise the prodrome and lie down / counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip), hydration and salt, avoid triggers/quick standing; and gives accurate driving advice for simple faints with warning (DVLA, updated September 2025: typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger, occurring when standing, lets a Group 1 driver continue without notifying the DVLA)
Hears the signposted health anxiety and treats reassurance as a skilled task — specific, evidence-based, and warm — not a dismissive "it’s just a faint"
Explores the specific fear (the ward patient) and the life-shrinking avoidance, so the reassurance is targeted at what she actually dreads

Safety-nets precisely so reassurance is safe: what WOULD change the picture and warrant review (faints without warning, during exertion, palpitations-then-collapse, injury) → come back; offers follow-up for the anxiety; leaves her with a diagnosis, a self-management plan, and her life back

worked.txt: "I want to start with the answer, because you’ve been carrying the question at 3am: what you’re describing is a classic simple faint — vasovagal syncope. I’m not guessing or being kind; the story fits it perfectly, and that confidence is the most useful thing I can give you today."

"Here’s why I’m sure. Every faint gave you warning — hot, sick, tunnel vision — and a quick recovery. They happened giving blood, standing in a hot ward, getting up fast when ill. That’s the textbook trigger list. The faints that worry me are the OPPOSITE: no warning, during exercise, or a racing heart first — and you’ve had none of those, your ECG’s normal, and there’s no young sudden death in your family. I’ve actively looked for the dangerous version and it isn’t here."

"On the brain scan — I understand the instinct, but let me be straight as one clinician to another: brain tumours don’t cause faints-with-warning like yours. A scan wouldn’t change this diagnosis, and an incidental finding would give us something new to worry about for no reason. The honest, evidence-based answer is that your story IS the test, and it’s reassuring."

"Can I ask what specifically frightened you into a brain tumour? … The patient on your ward, your age — that makes complete sense. You’ve seen how a serious illness can start, and your brain did the cruel thing of writing you into her story. But her funny turns and your faints are genuinely different things, and I can tell you why with confidence."

"Here’s what I think is actually happening to your life: the faints are harmless, but the FEAR of them has you not driving, off the gym, checking your pulse, not sleeping. That’s health anxiety, it’s incredibly common, and it’s treatable. The constant Googling and pulse-checking actually feeds it. Let’s get your life back, not just label the faints."

"For the faints: when you feel that hot, tunnel-vision warning, get down — sit or lie, cross your legs, clench your fists; keep well hydrated, a bit more salt, don’t spring up. For simple faints with warning you’re fine to drive. Come back if anything changes — a faint with NO warning, during exercise, or a thumping heart before you go. And I’d like to see you about the worry itself, because that’s the bit stealing your sleep. Deal?"

f.learning: Vasovagal syncope is a POSITIVE clinical diagnosis from the history — prodrome (hot, nauseated, tunnel vision, ringing ears), classic triggers (venepuncture, prolonged standing, heat, postural on illness), rapid full recovery — not a diagnosis of exclusion that requires scanning. The skill set is twofold. Clinically: make the diagnosis confidently while actively excluding (out loud) the red flags that mandate cardiac or neurological work-up — exertional/no-warning syncope, palpitations-then-collapse, syncope lying down, family history of young sudden death, seizure features. Communicationally: the real presentation is HEALTH ANXIETY, signposted and triggered by a ward patient her age with a brain tumour. Reassurance here is a skilled task — specific, evidence-based, warm — not "it’s just a faint". Explain why a scan would harm not help, find and address the specific fear and the life-shrinking avoidance, give vasovagal self-management (ESC 2018, international) and accurate driving advice (DVLA, September 2025: Group 1 need not notify for typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger when standing), offer NHS Talking Therapies for the health anxiety (stepped care; CG123 withdrawn 2024), and safety-net precisely so reassurance is safe.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG109 (updated 2023) · ESC syncope guidelines (2018) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025) · NICE CG113 · NICE CG123 (withdrawn May 2024)
knowledge.summary: Vasovagal syncope is a positive diagnosis made from the history: posture, a provoking factor and a prodrome, with rapid full recovery. With a normal ECG and no red flags she needs no further tests; the health anxiety is the problem to treat.

points.h: Make the diagnosis from the story
points.t: NICE CG109: diagnose uncomplicated faint when there are no features suggesting another diagnosis and the ‘3 Ps’ are present: posture (prolonged standing, or episodes prevented by lying down), provoking factors (such as pain or a medical procedure) and prodromal symptoms (such as sweating or feeling hot). If there is nothing else to raise clinical or social concern, no further immediate management is needed.
NICE CG109 recommends a 12-lead ECG for everyone with transient loss of consciousness. Hers is normal, which removes a major reason for referral.

points.h: Red flags to exclude out loud
points.t: NICE CG109: refer within 24 hours for specialist cardiovascular assessment if there is an ECG abnormality, heart failure, TLoC during exertion, a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Seizure pointers include a bitten tongue, head-turning, unusual posturing, prolonged jerking, and confusion afterwards.
A typical reflex faint needs no neuroimaging. CG109 advises against routine EEG, and ESC 2018 advises against brain imaging for uncomplicated syncope. An incidental finding would feed the anxiety.

ESC 2018: education and reassurance, recognising the prodrome, physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip, arm tensing) and lying down, avoiding triggers, and good fluid and salt intake. Lie down for procedures such as venepuncture.

Checking, reassurance-seeking and avoidance maintain health anxiety. Offer psychoeducation and self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies for CBT (stepped care; NICE CG113 if generalised anxiety; CG123 withdrawn 2024). DVLA (September 2025): typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger, occurring when standing, lets a Group 1 driver continue without notifying DVLA.

dg.d: Open question; acknowledged the fear and the scan request without agreeing to it or dismissing it.
Nurse on a busy ward; avoidance of driving and the gym; poor sleep; checking and Googling.
Reviewed the normal ECG and lying and standing BP; explained no scan or EEG is indicated (NICE CG109).
Reflex syncope vs orthostatic vs cardiac arrhythmia vs seizure; tested each with targeted questions.
Exertional, supine and no-warning syncope, palpitations, family history of young sudden death, and seizure features all asked and excluded out loud.
Confident positive diagnosis of vasovagal syncope, with health anxiety named as the main problem.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Counter-pressure manoeuvres, fluids and salt, trigger avoidance; accurate DVLA advice; talking therapy for health anxiety.
Health anxiety, sleep and avoidance addressed; lying down for venepuncture; hydration on long shifts.
Named the features that would need same-day review; follow-up booked in a few weeks for the anxiety.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (brain tumour or heart stopping), concern (the ward patient’s story), expectation (a brain scan).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Health anxiety with real life-shrinking avoidance is the true presentation — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.

model.text: Hello Casey, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining. You look tense. Tell me what’s been happening.
I’ve fainted three times and I’ve convinced myself something’s seriously wrong. A brain tumour, or my heart stopping. I’m a nurse, so I know just enough to scare myself. I think I need a brain scan.

I can hear how frightened you are, and I want to give you a proper answer, not a brush-off. Can I go through each faint in detail first? That will tell us more than anything else. Then I’ll explain what I think and we’ll talk about the scan.
model.why: Takes the fear seriously and sets an agenda that includes the scan request

model.text: Okay.
Take me through the first one. Where were you, and what did you feel just before?
Giving blood. I went hot and sweaty, felt sick, my vision went grey from the edges, then I was on the floor. I was back with it in seconds.
And the other two?
model.why: Checks the pattern is consistent across episodes

model.text: Standing through a long handover on a boiling ward. Same warning. And getting out of bed fast when I had a virus. Same again.
Have you ever fainted during exercise, while lying down, or with no warning at all? Any racing or pounding heart before you went?
No. Never. Always the hot, sick feeling first.
Did anyone see you jerk for a long time, did you bite the side of your tongue, wet yourself, or feel muddled for a long time afterwards?
No. Colleagues said I was out for a few seconds and then just embarrassed.
Has anyone in your family died suddenly or unexpectedly young, or had a heart condition that runs in families?
model.why: Family history of sudden cardiac death

model.text: No, nothing like that.
You said a brain tumour. What made you think of that in particular?
model.why: Explores the specific fear behind the scan request

model.text: There’s a woman on my ward, my age. Her brain tumour started with funny turns. I can’t stop thinking it’s me next.
That makes complete sense. You’ve seen how it went for her, and your mind has put you into her story. How has the worry been affecting your life?
model.why: Validates the fear and explores its impact

model.text: I’ve stopped driving. I’ve stopped the gym. I check my pulse constantly and I’m awake at three Googling.

I want to give you the answer first, because you’ve been carrying the question at three in the morning. This is a simple faint, called vasovagal syncope. I’m not saying that to be kind. Your story fits it exactly.
How can you be sure without a scan?

Every faint had a trigger: a needle, standing in heat, getting up fast when unwell. Every one had the warning and a quick recovery. The faints that worry doctors are the opposite: no warning, during exercise, lying down, or a racing heart first. You’ve had none of those, your heart tracing is normal and there’s no sudden death in your family. I looked for the dangerous version and it isn’t there.
model.why: Shows the reasoning and states the excluded red flags

model.text: But the patient on my ward…

Brain tumours don’t cause faints with a warning and a trigger like yours. A scan wouldn’t change the diagnosis, and scans often show small harmless things that would give you something new to worry about. As one clinician to another: your story is the test, and it’s reassuring.
model.why: Explains why a scan is not indicated without dismissing her

model.text: For the faints themselves: when the hot, grey feeling starts, get down straight away. Sit or lie, cross your legs and squeeze, or grip your hands together. Drink plenty, don’t skip meals, take a bit more salt, and don’t spring out of bed. Lie down when you give blood.
And driving? I’ve been too scared.

For a simple faint like yours, with a clear trigger and warning when you’re standing, you can drive and you don’t need to tell the DVLA. If you ever felt that warning at the wheel, you’d pull over safely.
model.why: Accurate DVLA advice for reflex syncope

model.text: That’s a relief, actually.

The bigger thing, I think, is the worry. The faints are harmless, but the fear has taken your driving, the gym and your sleep. That’s health anxiety. It’s common and very treatable, and the pulse-checking and Googling keep it going. Would you be open to talking therapy? You can refer yourself, and I’d like to see you in a few weeks to see how you are.
model.why: Names the health anxiety and agrees a plan for it

model.text: Yes. I think I need that more than a scan, if I’m honest.

What would change my mind and bring you back quickly: a faint with no warning, during exercise or while lying down, a racing heart before you go, or a faint where you injure yourself. Any of those, contact us the same day.
model.why: Precise safety-net that keeps reassurance safe

model.text: Okay.
If a colleague asked you tomorrow what the GP said, what would you tell them?
That they’re simple faints, the story proves it, I don’t need a scan, and I get down when I feel it coming. And I’m sorting out the anxiety.
Perfect. Let’s get your life back.
model.why: Closes with a clear, hopeful message

social.t: Stopped driving and the gym, sleeping badly, checking her pulse. The life shrinking around the fear is the main harm.
Long shifts on hot wards without breaks or fluids are triggers. Hydration, eating and sitting when possible help; occupational health can advise if faints at work continue.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025): typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger, occurring when standing, lets a Group 1 driver continue without notifying DVLA. Syncope without warning, while sitting, or while driving needs the relevant DVLA standard.

professional.t: She is a patient first. Avoid shortcuts because she is a nurse, and give the same full history, explanation and safety-net as for anyone else.
Declining a scan that is not indicated is good practice when explained with reasons and alternatives (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024; GMC Decision making and consent 2020). Document the discussion.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for health anxiety; STARS (Syncope Trust and Reflex Anoxic Seizures) for patient information on reflex syncope.

redFlags: Syncope during exertion, while lying down, or with no warning: cardiac cause until proven otherwise
Palpitations before collapse, abnormal ECG, heart murmur, new breathlessness, family history of sudden death under 40: specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109)
Tongue-biting, prolonged jerking, head-turning or prolonged confusion: consider epilepsy
psychosocial: Nurse who ‘knows enough to scare herself’
Avoidance of driving and exercise; poor sleep
Pulse-checking and Googling as maintaining behaviours
ice: Idea: a brain tumour or her heart stopping
Concern: a ward patient her age whose tumour started with funny turns
Expectation: a brain scan and to be told she is not dying

playbook.diagnosis: Recurrent vasovagal (reflex) syncope: typical triggers (venepuncture, prolonged standing in heat, postural during illness), prodrome and rapid recovery, normal ECG and lying and standing BP, no red flags. Significant health anxiety with avoidance.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A simple faint is your body’s reflex overreacting: your heart slows and blood vessels widen for a moment, so less blood reaches your brain and you go down. Lying flat fixes it, which is why you came round in seconds. It isn’t dangerous and it isn’t a sign of anything in your brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve seen what happened to the patient on your ward, and your mind put you in her story. Your faints are a different thing, and I can show you why.”
management.psychosocial: Name the health anxiety; self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies; plan to return to driving and the gym; reduce checking and Googling.
sharedPlan: Confident diagnosis of vasovagal syncope; no scan or further tests (NICE CG109)
Counter-pressure manoeuvres, lying down at the prodrome, fluids and salt, lie down for venepuncture (ESC 2018)
May drive without notifying DVLA (DVLA, September 2025); talking therapy for health anxiety
safetyNet: Same-day review for faints with no warning, on exertion, lying down, with palpitations, or with injury
Follow-up in a few weeks for the anxiety

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether reassurance can be delivered as a clinical skill. It is failed both by the candidate who orders a scan to calm her and by the one who says “it’s just a faint” and moves on.

items.fail: Ordering a CT or MRI head to put her mind at rest.
items.why: Not indicated for uncomplicated faint (NICE CG109; ESC 2018), and it reinforces health anxiety.
items.fix: Explain why the story is the test and what a scan could and could not tell her.

items.fail: Diagnosing vasovagal syncope without asking about exertion, lying down, palpitations or family history.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The reassurance is only safe if the red flags are excluded.
items.fix: Ask each red flag and then say out loud which ones you checked.

items.fail: “You’re a nurse, you know it’s just a faint.”
items.why: Dismissive; it ignores the specific fear and the ward patient.
items.fix: Ask what made her think of a tumour, then address that story directly.

items.fail: Telling her not to drive, or to inform the DVLA.
items.why: Incorrect: DVLA (September 2025) allows a Group 1 driver with typical vasovagal syncope and an avoidable trigger when standing to drive without notifying.
items.fix: Give the correct rule and what would change it.

items.fail: Ignoring the anxiety because the faints are benign.
items.why: The avoidance and sleeplessness are the real morbidity; leaving them misses her agenda.
items.fix: Name health anxiety, explain how checking maintains it, and offer talking therapy and follow-up.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: It will happen again; that advice brings her straight back into the anxiety cycle.
items.fix: Name what would change the picture: no warning, exertion, lying down, palpitations, injury.

Each faint: posture, trigger, prodrome, recovery. Then red flags: exertion, lying down, no warning, palpitations, seizure features, family history.
The ward patient her age. The avoidance: no driving, no gym, pulse-checking, sleepless nights.
Confident diagnosis with the reasoning shown. Why no scan. Counter-pressure manoeuvres and fluids. DVLA. Name the health anxiety and offer talking therapy.
What would change the picture. Follow-up booked. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Orders a brain scan to settle her, or says “it’s just a faint” without showing any reasoning; never asks about exertional or supine syncope or family history; ignores the anxiety and the avoidance.
wordPics.pass: Makes a clear diagnosis of vasovagal syncope from the history, asks about the red flags, explains why a scan is not needed, gives self-management advice and a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: states the excluded red flags out loud so the reassurance is credible; finds the ward patient and addresses that fear directly; names the health anxiety and agrees a plan for it; accurate DVLA advice that lets her drive again; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s just a faint, nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “Here’s why I’m sure: every faint had a trigger and a warning, and none had the features that worry doctors.”
avoid.why: Flat reassurance without reasoning does not land with an anxious clinician.

avoid.dont: “I’ll request a scan just to put your mind at rest.”
avoid.instead: “A scan wouldn’t change the diagnosis and might find something harmless that worries you more. Your story is the test.”
avoid.why: Unnecessary investigation reinforces health anxiety and is not in line with guidance.

avoid.dont: “You shouldn’t drive until this is sorted.”
avoid.instead: “For a simple faint like yours, you can drive and don’t need to tell the DVLA.”
avoid.why: Incorrect driving advice adds to her avoidance.

SCA_MODELS.text: For the faints themselves: when the hot, grey feeling starts, get down straight away. Sit or lie, cross your legs and squeeze, or grip your hands together. Drink plenty, don’t skip meals, take a bit more salt, and don’t spring out of bed. Lie down when you give blood.
And driving? I’ve been too scared.

For a simple faint like yours, with a clear trigger and warning when you’re standing, you can drive and you don’t need to tell the DVLA. If you ever felt that warning at the wheel, you’d pull over safely.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate DVLA advice for reflex syncope

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s a relief, actually.

The bigger thing, I think, is the worry. The faints are harmless, but the fear has taken your driving, the gym and your sleep. That’s health anxiety. It’s common and very treatable, and the pulse-checking and Googling keep it going. Would you be open to talking therapy? You can refer yourself, and I’d like to see you in a few weeks to see how you are.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the health anxiety and agrees a plan for it

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I think I need that more than a scan, if I’m honest.

What would change my mind and bring you back quickly: a faint with no warning, during exercise or while lying down, a racing heart before you go, or a faint where you injure yourself. Any of those, contact us the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Precise safety-net that keeps reassurance safe

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
If a colleague asked you tomorrow what the GP said, what would you tell them?
That they’re simple faints, the story proves it, I don’t need a scan, and I get down when I feel it coming. And I’m sorting out the anxiety.
Perfect. Let’s get your life back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with a clear, hopeful message

SCA_STEM.name: Casey Doyle
SCA_STEM.recent: Three faints in 4 months: giving blood, standing at a hot ward handover, and rising quickly from bed during a viral illness. 12-lead ECG last week: normal. Lying and standing BP in clinic: normal.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about recurrent fainting. Requesting a brain scan.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG109 (updated 2023) · ESC syncope guidelines (2018) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025) · NICE CG113 · NICE CG123 (withdrawn May 2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Vasovagal syncope is a positive diagnosis made from the history: posture, a provoking factor and a prodrome, with rapid full recovery. With a normal ECG and no red flags she needs no further tests; the health anxiety is the problem to treat.

points.h: Make the diagnosis from the story
points.t: NICE CG109: diagnose uncomplicated faint when there are no features suggesting another diagnosis and the ‘3 Ps’ are present: posture (prolonged standing, or episodes prevented by lying down), provoking factors (such as pain or a medical procedure) and prodromal symptoms (such as sweating or feeling hot). If there is nothing else to raise clinical or social concern, no further immediate management is needed.
NICE CG109 recommends a 12-lead ECG for everyone with transient loss of consciousness. Hers is normal, which removes a major reason for referral.

points.h: Red flags to exclude out loud
points.t: NICE CG109: refer within 24 hours for specialist cardiovascular assessment if there is an ECG abnormality, heart failure, TLoC during exertion, a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Seizure pointers include a bitten tongue, head-turning, unusual posturing, prolonged jerking, and confusion afterwards.
A typical reflex faint needs no neuroimaging. CG109 advises against routine EEG, and ESC 2018 advises against brain imaging for uncomplicated syncope. An incidental finding would feed the anxiety.

ESC 2018: education and reassurance, recognising the prodrome, physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (leg crossing, hand grip, arm tensing) and lying down, avoiding triggers, and good fluid and salt intake. Lie down for procedures such as venepuncture.

Checking, reassurance-seeking and avoidance maintain health anxiety. Offer psychoeducation and self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies for CBT (stepped care; NICE CG113 if generalised anxiety; CG123 withdrawn 2024). DVLA (September 2025): typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger, occurring when standing, lets a Group 1 driver continue without notifying DVLA.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the fear and the scan request without agreeing to it or dismissing it.
Nurse on a busy ward; avoidance of driving and the gym; poor sleep; checking and Googling.
Picked up “I know just enough to scare myself” and the patient ‘her age’, and explored both.
Idea (brain tumour or heart stopping), concern (the ward patient’s story), expectation (a brain scan).
Reviewed the normal ECG and lying and standing BP; explained no scan or EEG is indicated (NICE CG109).
Reflex syncope vs orthostatic vs cardiac arrhythmia vs seizure; tested each with targeted questions.
Exertional, supine and no-warning syncope, palpitations, family history of young sudden death, and seizure features all asked and excluded out loud.
Confident positive diagnosis of vasovagal syncope, with health anxiety named as the main problem.
Counter-pressure manoeuvres, fluids and salt, trigger avoidance; accurate DVLA advice; talking therapy for health anxiety.
Health anxiety, sleep and avoidance addressed; lying down for venepuncture; hydration on long shifts.
Named the features that would need same-day review; follow-up booked in a few weeks for the anxiety.

social.t: Stopped driving and the gym, sleeping badly, checking her pulse. The life shrinking around the fear is the main harm.
Long shifts on hot wards without breaks or fluids are triggers. Hydration, eating and sitting when possible help; occupational health can advise if faints at work continue.

legal.t: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (updated September 2025): typical vasovagal syncope with an avoidable trigger, occurring when standing, lets a Group 1 driver continue without notifying DVLA. Syncope without warning, while sitting, or while driving needs the relevant DVLA standard.

professional.t: She is a patient first. Avoid shortcuts because she is a nurse, and give the same full history, explanation and safety-net as for anyone else.
Declining a scan that is not indicated is good practice when explained with reasons and alternatives (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024; GMC Decision making and consent 2020). Document the discussion.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for health anxiety; STARS (Syncope Trust and Reflex Anoxic Seizures) for patient information on reflex syncope.

redFlags: Syncope during exertion, while lying down, or with no warning: cardiac cause until proven otherwise
Palpitations before collapse, abnormal ECG, heart murmur, new breathlessness, family history of sudden death under 40: specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109)
Tongue-biting, prolonged jerking, head-turning or prolonged confusion: consider epilepsy
psychosocial: Nurse who ‘knows enough to scare herself’
Avoidance of driving and exercise; poor sleep
Pulse-checking and Googling as maintaining behaviours
ice: Idea: a brain tumour or her heart stopping
Concern: a ward patient her age whose tumour started with funny turns
Expectation: a brain scan and to be told she is not dying

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Recurrent vasovagal (reflex) syncope: typical triggers (venepuncture, prolonged standing in heat, postural during illness), prodrome and rapid recovery, normal ECG and lying and standing BP, no red flags. Significant health anxiety with avoidance.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A simple faint is your body’s reflex overreacting: your heart slows and blood vessels widen for a moment, so less blood reaches your brain and you go down. Lying flat fixes it, which is why you came round in seconds. It isn’t dangerous and it isn’t a sign of anything in your brain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve seen what happened to the patient on your ward, and your mind put you in her story. Your faints are a different thing, and I can show you why.”
management.psychosocial: Name the health anxiety; self-referral to NHS Talking Therapies; plan to return to driving and the gym; reduce checking and Googling.
sharedPlan: Confident diagnosis of vasovagal syncope; no scan or further tests (NICE CG109)
Counter-pressure manoeuvres, lying down at the prodrome, fluids and salt, lie down for venepuncture (ESC 2018)
May drive without notifying DVLA (DVLA, September 2025); talking therapy for health anxiety
safetyNet: Same-day review for faints with no warning, on exertion, lying down, with palpitations, or with injury
Follow-up in a few weeks for the anxiety

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether reassurance can be delivered as a clinical skill. It is failed both by the candidate who orders a scan to calm her and by the one who says “it’s just a faint” and moves on.

items.fail: Ordering a CT or MRI head to put her mind at rest.
items.why: Not indicated for uncomplicated faint (NICE CG109; ESC 2018), and it reinforces health anxiety.
items.fix: Explain why the story is the test and what a scan could and could not tell her.

items.fail: Diagnosing vasovagal syncope without asking about exertion, lying down, palpitations or family history.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The reassurance is only safe if the red flags are excluded.
items.fix: Ask each red flag and then say out loud which ones you checked.

items.fail: “You’re a nurse, you know it’s just a faint.”
items.why: Dismissive; it ignores the specific fear and the ward patient.
items.fix: Ask what made her think of a tumour, then address that story directly.

items.fail: Telling her not to drive, or to inform the DVLA.
items.why: Incorrect: DVLA (September 2025) allows a Group 1 driver with typical vasovagal syncope and an avoidable trigger when standing to drive without notifying.
items.fix: Give the correct rule and what would change it.

items.fail: Ignoring the anxiety because the faints are benign.
items.why: The avoidance and sleeplessness are the real morbidity; leaving them misses her agenda.
items.fix: Name health anxiety, explain how checking maintains it, and offer talking therapy and follow-up.

items.fail: Safety-netting with “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: It will happen again; that advice brings her straight back into the anxiety cycle.
items.fix: Name what would change the picture: no warning, exertion, lying down, palpitations, injury.
